A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoRAN, with matching authors, attack algorithm, benchmarks, and examples despite the changed title. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and their tables, figures, and mathematical content support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack success rates, query counts, external-judge evaluations, and attack examples across three benchmarks and three victim models.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, additional victim models and judges, resource measurements, refinement analyses, and a defensive alignment experiment.

M1.justification: The attack algorithm and appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged. However, Section 4.6 adds a defensive training procedure: construct preferences from AutoRAN attacks, mix FalseReject data, train a reward model, and align Qwen3-8B using Dr. GRPO/RLHF. This substantially extends the proposed procedures beyond attacking models.

E1.justification: AdvBench, HarmBench, and StrongReject are retained. v2 adds FalseReject data for defensive training and XSTest for evaluating excessive refusals, extending coverage from harmful-request attacks to model alignment and benign-request handling.

E2.justification: v1 contains no evaluated competing attack baseline. v2 directly evaluates MouseTrap and AutoDAN-Turbo in Appendix A.3 and adds an original-data RLHF comparator in Table 4. H-CoT supplies a judging protocol only; v2 explicitly states that an end-to-end H-CoT attack comparison was unavailable.

E3.justification: The original 50/50/54 benchmark counts and ten-turn attack budget are retained. v2 adds DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-8B victim configurations, LLaMA Guard classification and MouseTrap/H-CoT judging criteria, resource accounting including warm-up comparisons, and a defensive train/test evaluation with an over-refusal metric.

E4.justification: v2 expands robustness checks across judging standards, adds refinement-case frequency analyses in Tables 1 and 10, and evaluates defensive alignment alongside over-refusal. The original score-distribution analysis and detailed attack examples are retained, although relocated. The refinement analysis is observational; no experiment removing access to reasoning traces is reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Added averages and judge comparisons do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original ASR entries and Figure 4 turn distributions are retained. Newly reported results include LLaMA Guard rates of 62.0–96.3%, 100% ASR on the additional victim models, and 100% versus 74% against AutoDAN-Turbo on Qwen3-8B/HarmBench. Table 4 newly reports defensive alignment reducing AutoRAN ASR from 100% to 8%, with XSTest over-refusal increasing from 9.2% to 10.8%. Cost and refinement-frequency results are also added.

T1.justification: Table 8 adds explicit mathematical definitions of token and time ratios as MouseTrap resource use divided by AutoRAN resource use. This is a limited metric-definition addition; the existing threat-model formalization is retained, and no theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical derivation is added.

C1.justification: v2 reframes the principal novelty from automated weak-to-strong jailbreaking to automated hijacking of safety reasoning. It also adds a substantive contribution claim in the introduction: AutoRAN-generated training data can improve alignment, supported by the newly reported 92% attack-success reduction. The original high-success attack claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that external judging excludes an attacker-judge artifact, that refinement is essential against stronger defenses, and that hiding reasoning traces would prevent many attacks. It also interprets AutoRAN as a defensive training resource and replaces v1's unexplored-defense limitation with discussion of an ongoing transparency–security tension. The hidden-trace counterfactual is asserted without a corresponding controlled experiment.

D1.justification: v2 discloses 500 attack-response pairs and balanced FalseReject mixing for the defense, but leaves its split proportions and training hyperparameters unspecified. It removes v1's NVIDIA A6000/vLLM disclosure, exact first-prompt selection rules, and statement that running records are available. The code link, algorithm, and detailed attack prompts remain.

R1.justification: The related-work survey and principal relationships to H-CoT, MouseTrap, PAIR, and Weak-to-Strong are largely retained, with emphasis shifted toward safety-reasoning hijacking. Focused references are added for LLaMA Guard, AutoDAN-Turbo, Dr. GRPO, FalseReject, and XSTest; the vLLM reference is removed. Bibliographic restyling does not constitute additional research coverage.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, method framing, evaluation narrative, case-study explanations, and conclusion. It introduces execution-hijacking terminology, condenses existing explanations, reorganizes evaluation sections, and inserts an additional-results appendix before the retained algorithm, prompts, and examples.

P2.justification: v2 restructures and expands the original ASR table and adds nine tables covering judges, comparisons, costs, defense, and refinement frequencies. The original score-distribution Figure 5 becomes appendix Figure 6, while the case-study Figure 6 becomes Figure 5. Typography, spacing, and figure placement change throughout; the principal existing graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: The direct baseline comparisons, additional judging standards, and defense/over-refusal evaluation improve empirical context beyond v1's standalone attack demonstration. The gain is limited by new inconsistencies: Section 4.2 claims 98–100% under H-CoT although Tables 2 and 6 include 84%, and Table 10 reports 26% Case 2 refinement for Gemini/HarmBench despite Figure 4 showing 49 of 50 attacks succeeding immediately. Sparse defense-training documentation and removal of earlier hardware and sampling details also weaken reproducibility.
